To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the use of amateur annotations for hate speech detection can result in lower accuracy and higher false positive rate; and (b) the use of expert annotations for training a classifier can result in higher accuracy and lower false positive rate.
1) expert annotations are more accurate than amateur annotations, and 2) systems trained on expert data are more accurate than systems trained on amateur data.

1) amateur annotators are likely to label tweets as hate speech more frequently than expert annotators, and 2) systems trained on expert annotated data sets outperform systems trained with data sets that are annotated by amateurs.

the following question: Are you a racist or am I seeing things?

the question of how to create a data set for hate speech detection that is both large and of high quality, and we find that the answer to this question may be to use both expert and amateur annotators.
the question of whether or not we can rely on the annotations of non-expert annotators in hate speech detection. We conclude that we can, but that the quality of the data will suffer.
